headline: Kenya gets ready for strong El Niño floods

sources.title: El Niño in Kenya: 'It can kill us,' says Nairobi resident (BBC News)
Forecasts of El Niño floods have mobilized a 'Green Army' (NPR)

chunks.text: A 62-year-old woman lives in one of Kenya's largest [[informal settlements]], poor neighborhoods built without plans or [[permits]]. Her home in Nairobi, the capital, is a few meters from a river. In March 2026, [[floodwater]] rose halfway up its metal walls. Her sister {{passed away}} in those floods. Homes on [[riverbanks]] like hers can be {{washed away}} in [[flash floods]]. In a news report on November 11, 2026, she said she fears new floods.

verbs.correct: To die (a polite way to say it)
verbs.wrong: To be badly hurt in a storm
verbs.why: Many people pass away in the hospital. When a pet passes away, the whole family feels sad. The woman's sister passed away in the floods in March 2026.

verbs.correct: To destroy or remove with moving water
verbs.wrong: To be built from mud and sticks
verbs.why: Heavy rain often washes away the sand on this beach. A strong flood can wash away a small bridge. In Nairobi, homes on riverbanks can be washed away in flash floods.

chunks.text: The reason is El Niño, a natural [[weather pattern]] in which part of the Pacific Ocean becomes warmer than usual. U.S. scientists called it "very strong" in September 2026. In East Africa, it usually brings [[heavier rain]]. Kenya has two [[rainy seasons]]. The shorter one usually runs from October to December. By November 11, the heaviest rains had not {{set in}} yet. Since August, the government has {{stepped up}} work on rivers and drains to {{head off}} a disaster.

verbs.wrong: To fall only in one small area
verbs.why: In our town, the cold sets in every November. The rains set in, and the roads turn to mud. By November 11, 2026, the heaviest El Niño rains had not set in yet.

verbs.wrong: To move work to a new place
verbs.why: Police step up patrols before big games. Stores step up hiring before the busy season. Since August 2026, Kenya's government has stepped up work to clean rivers and drains.

verbs.correct: To stop something before it happens
verbs.wrong: To report something on the news
verbs.why: A quick talk often heads off a big fight. Good tires help head off accidents on wet roads. Kenya is cleaning its rivers and drains to head off a flood disaster.

chunks.text: In Nairobi, workers in [[bright vests]] are {{digging trash out}} of rivers and [[drains]]. A city [[youth jobs program]] with more than 4,000 workers is helping. Plastic bottles and other trash often {{pile up}} in the water. Then rainwater {{backs up}} into the streets. Nairobi's head of disaster planning says the [[drainage system]] was built 30 years ago for about 2.5 million people. It has not {{kept up with}} a [[daytime population]] of about 7 million.

verbs.correct: To remove something with a shovel
verbs.why: Every winter, my neighbors dig their cars out of the snow. The kids dig old toys out of the sand at the beach. In Nairobi, workers are digging trash out of rivers and drains.

verbs.correct: To collect until there is a lot
verbs.wrong: To lose its color in water
verbs.why: Dirty dishes pile up when I work late. Leaves pile up in the yard every fall. Plastic bottles and other trash often pile up in Nairobi's rivers.

verbs.correct: To collect because a drain is blocked
verbs.wrong: To dry quickly in the hot sun
verbs.why: When the kitchen sink is blocked, water backs up into it. Rainwater backs up when leaves fill the gutters. In Nairobi, rainwater backs up into the streets when drains are blocked.

verbs.correct: To grow as fast as something else
verbs.wrong: To cost less than something else
verbs.why: Our small school never keeps up with the number of new students. Pay often does not keep up with rising prices. Nairobi's old drainage system has not kept up with the city's fast growth.

chunks.text: Workers have also {{torn down}} [[food stalls]] built without permits. The same official says about 100,000 people could be [[at risk]] in the [[worst case]]. The city has {{set aside}} 167 sites where families who must leave will get food and [[supplies]]. Officials told her to leave until the rains pass. But she {{gets by}} on about 2 dollars a day, selling peanuts and fruit, so she cannot afford to move.

verbs.correct: To destroy a building on purpose
verbs.wrong: To close a shop for one day
verbs.why: The town tears down old houses that are not safe. Cities tear down empty buildings to make room for parks. In Nairobi, workers have torn down food stalls built without permits.

verbs.correct: To keep something for a special use
verbs.wrong: To build something in a hurry
verbs.why: Many families set aside money for a new car. Our school sets aside one room for quiet study. Nairobi has set aside 167 sites where families who must leave will get food and supplies.

verbs.correct: To have just enough money to live
verbs.why: Many students get by on a small part-time job. My grandmother gets by on a small pension. The woman in Nairobi gets by on about 2 dollars a day, selling peanuts and fruit.

mainIdea.s: A very strong El Niño may bring floods to Kenya during its short rainy season. Nairobi is cleaning rivers and drains, but many poor families living near water still face real danger.
mainIdea.why: Forecasters warn that El Niño could bring new floods. Workers are digging trash out of rivers and drains, but riverside homes can still be washed away.

mainIdea.s: Kenya plans to protect its capital from El Niño by building a brand-new set of pipes under every street. Officials promise the work will be finished before the heavy rains arrive there.
mainIdea.why: Close, but workers are cleaning rivers and old drains, which have not kept up with the city's growth. Those drains were built 30 years ago for far fewer people.

mainIdea.s: A long dry spell has left farmers in northern Kenya with little water for their animals. Aid groups are sending trucks of water to villages as the government asks other nations for help.
mainIdea.why: This is about getting ready for El Niño floods. Nairobi has stepped up work on its rivers and drains before the heavy rains set in.

tf.s: A woman in Nairobi fears new floods because her home is near a river.
tf.why: Her small home is a few meters from a river, and homes on riverbanks can be washed away in flash floods.

tf.s: The heavy El Niño rains have already set in and flooded Nairobi.
tf.why: The floods are only forecast. By November 11, 2026, the heaviest rains had not set in yet.

tf.s: Kenya's government has stepped up work on its rivers and drains.
tf.why: Since August, it has stepped up the work to head off a disaster before the heavy rains.

tf.s: Nairobi's drains have easily kept up with the city's fast growth.
tf.why: The drains were built for about 2.5 million people, so they have not kept up with about 7 million.

tf.s: Trash that piles up in drains can make rainwater back up into streets.
tf.why: Plastic bottles and other trash pile up in the water, and blocked drains make rainwater back up into the streets.

tf.s: The woman can easily pay to leave her riverside home for a while.
tf.why: She gets by on about 2 dollars a day selling peanuts and fruit, so she cannot afford to move.

lines.text: Did you see that story about El Niño and Kenya?
I did. I thought the rains hadn't {{set in}} yet.
They haven't, but forecasters say this El Niño is very strong. People there have to [[prepare for the worst]].
So what is Nairobi actually doing?
Teams of workers are {{digging trash out}} of the rivers and drains.
Why does that matter so much?
Trash {{piles up}}, the drains get blocked, and the water {{backs up}} into the streets.
And the drains are 30 years old, right? They were never going to {{keep up with}} seven million people.
Exactly. The government has {{stepped up}} the work since August to {{head off}} another disaster.
[[Not a moment too soon]]. The floods in March were really bad.
They were. The woman in the story said her sister {{passed away}} in those floods.
That's so sad. [[I can only imagine]] how scared she is now.
Officials told her to leave her home by the river until the rains pass.
[[That's just it]]. She {{gets by}} on about two dollars a day, so she can't pay for another place.
Wow. She's really [[in a tough spot]].
The city has {{set aside}} 167 sites where families who must leave can get food and supplies.
Good. Homes on the riverbanks could get {{washed away}}.

expressions.def: Used to say that people must get ready for the worst thing that could happen
ex: The doctors told the family to prepare for the worst.
When the storm turned toward us, we had to prepare for the worst.

expressions.def: Used to say that something happened when it was badly needed, almost too late
ex: The plumber came not a moment too soon. Water was all over the floor.
We reached the shelter not a moment too soon, just as the storm hit.

expressions.def: Used to show that you understand how hard or strong a feeling must be
ex: You worked two jobs and studied? I can only imagine how tired you were.

expressions.def: Used to say that this is exactly the problem
ex: I want to buy a house. That's just it, though: prices are too high.
He needs to rest, but that's just it. He can't take a day off.

expressions.def: In a hard situation with no easy answer
ex: He is in a tough spot because his car broke down far from home.
Losing her job put her in a tough spot.
